title: How To Improve Classroom Management Every Day very-day/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin introduces a daily feedback strategy he calls "The List" for continuously improving classroom management rather than merely maintaining it. Teachers keep a simple sheet, divided into what went well and what needs work, noting specific routines and behaviors observed each day — from smooth transitions to talking during independent work. The following morning, the teacher briefly and matter-of-factly shares both lists with the class, offering specific praise for successes and clear, unemotional notes on what needs improvement, without lecturing, threatening, or over-praising. Linsin frames this as a form of honest, direct feedback that reinforces students' understanding of the teacher's standard and gives them something concrete to improve daily. Over time, he argues, the "needs work" list shrinks as the class moves steadily closer to the teacher's vision, generating intrinsic pride and motivation along the way.
points: Effective classroom management requires actively pushing for daily improvement, not merely maintaining acceptable behavior.
"The List" strategy tracks both what went well and what needs work each day on a simple daily sheet.
Sharing both lists briefly and matter-of-factly each morning reinforces the teacher's standard without lecturing or over-praising.
Specific, honest feedback — not vague praise or threats — is what moves a class steadily toward the teacher's vision.
Over time, the "needs work" list shrinks as students internalize the standard, generating intrinsic pride and motivation.
quotes: One of the secrets to exceptional classroom management is to aim for the stars.
But you mustn’t settle for just okay. You mustn’t merely hope to keep a lid on your classroom.
The way it works is that you’re going to keep a short daily list of the routines, behaviors, and activities that were done perfectly as well as a list of the areas that need work.
You won’t add a lecture. You won’t threaten or feign disappointment. You won’t over-praise, raise your voice, or give anything but the unvarnished truth.

Feedback, in the form of letting students know directly and honestly how they’re doing, and if what they’re doing is, indeed, how you taught them, is a little-known key to effective classroom management.
It moves your class closer and closer to your dream destination—until the bottom list all but disappears.
There is deep pride in doing things well, in seeing evidence of progress, in getting better every day through the pursuit of excellence.
